questions.question: Which three ways of taking blood does the chapter describe?
options: Venesection, leeches, and cupping
Cautery, ligature, and amputation
Purging, sweating, and fasting
Fasting, anointing, and bathing
questions.explanation: Venesection opens a vein, leeches do the measuring themselves, and cupping draws skin and sometimes blood into a heated cup.

questions.question: How did wet cupping differ from dry cupping?
options: It used cold water instead of a heated cup
It added small cuts so blood entered the cup
It used leeches inside the cup
It was done only on the scalp
questions.explanation: Dry cupping raised a bruise. Wet cupping added small cuts so blood entered the cup.

questions.question: What did Celsus note about bleeding the young, the old, and the pregnant?
options: He bled them more than anyone else
He said only priests could bleed them
It had once been forbidden and then became more common
He thought leeches were the only safe method
questions.explanation: Celsus notes that bleeding these groups had once been forbidden and then became more common. His caution about children is the humane note in a dangerous habit.

questions.question: Why did bloodletting seem to work?
options: It removed germs from the blood
It lowered blood sugar
It was always combined with antibiotics
Many acute diseases end in a few days regardless, and the patient may feel briefly cooler
questions.explanation: A feverish patient may feel a brief coolness after losing blood, and many acute diseases end on their own. Failures were explained as too little, too late, or the wrong day.

questions.question: Until when did bloodletting remain respectable in Europe?
options: The fifth century
The nineteenth century
The twelfth century
It was abandoned soon after Celsus
questions.explanation: The practice was already old in 30 AD and stayed respectable in Europe until the nineteenth century, a warning about how long a coherent error can live.
